parole.significato: Suffix used to form agent nouns (both animate and inanimate) from verbs in -и́ровать (-írovatʹ), -ирова́ть (-irovátʹ) a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ātor, from -tor added to verbs in -āre. Influenced by French -ateur, itself a borrowing from the same Latin suffix.
From Latin -ātiō, an alternative form of -tiō.

parole.significato: forms names of chemical elements, especially metallic ones: -ium
parole.testo: Reanalysis of Latin and New Latin terms suffixed with Latin -um or -ium.

parole.significato: augur, soothsayer (diviner who foretells events by unusual occurrences)

From Latin administrātor (via Polish administrator or German Administrator, the latter strongly denied by Shansky).

Borrowed from Latin amplitūdō, from Latin amplus.

parole.significato: animation (causing images to appear to move)

parole.significato: appeal (application for the removal of a cause to a superior judge for reexamination)

parole.significato: aperture (something which restricts the diameter of the light path through one plane in an optical system)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin apertura. Doublet of увертю́ра (uvertjúra).

parole.significato: to applaud, to cheer, to clap

From вода́ (vodá) + -о- (-o-) + боя́знь (bojáznʹ), a calque of Latin hydrophobia.

From Latin Gepidae, from Gothic *𐌲𐌹𐌱𐌹𐌸𐍃 (*gibiþs), from Proto-Germanic *gibidōz (which see for more).

parole.testo: From Latin Hermaphrodītus, from Ancient Greek Ἑρμαφρόδῑτος (Hermaphródītos).
Borrowed from Latin gerundium. See ерунда́ (jerundá) (a possible doublet). Compare natively formed Polish rzeczownik, odsłownik, Slovene glagolnik.

parole.significato: hydraulics (engineering science that deals with liquid in motion)

From Latin hypocaustum, from Ancient Greek ὑπό (hupó, “underneath”) + καυστόν (kaustón, “burnt offering”).

parole.significato: vocative (relating to the case used to express the person to which one is calling)
parole.testo: From звать (zvatʹ, “to call”) + -тельный (-telʹnyj, verbal adjective—forming suffix), a calque of Latin vōcātīvus.

parole.significato: epithalamium (poetic work in the nature of a panegyric on the occasion of a wedding)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin epithalamium, in turn from Ancient Greek ἐπιθαλάμιον (epithalámion), neuter form of Ancient Greek ἐπιθαλάμιος (epithalámios), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + θάλαμος (thálamos, “inner chamber, wedding chamber”).
Borrowed from Latin etymologia, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμολογία (etumología), from ἔτυμον (étumon, “true sense”) and -λογία (-logía, “study of”) (from λόγος (lógos)).
